episode_case.narrative: A healthy non-diabetic, 32-year old white woman started a low carbohydrate, high fat diet when she was breastfeeding her son of 10 months of age. After 10 days she was admitted to our hospital with nausea and vomiting and a serum pH of 7.20 and base excess of −19. Clinical signs and blood samples were compatible with ketoacidosis. She was given fluids intravenously and insulin. No anamnestic or clinical signs of diabetes were found. She recovered quickly and was discharged 3 days later.

anatomy.title: Starvation-induced ketoacidosis in breastfeeding
anatomy.explanation: Low carbohydrate intake forces the body to break down fat for energy, producing ketones. Breastfeeding increases metabolic demand, exacerbating ketone production.

script_stage.topic: A healthy breastfeeding woman unexpectedly developed a serious condition after starting a low-carb diet, despite not having diabetes.

script_result.script:
The woman in bed four had nursed her newborn at dawn, her milk rich and warm. By noon, her breath smelled of nail-polish remover. The first doctor called it stress. The second blamed a stomach bug. The third sent her home with antacids. None checked her blood for ketones—until the fourth physician, Dr. Elena Vasquez, caught the faint sweetness on her own tongue and ordered the test. The strips turned purple within seconds. The woman’s body, starved of carbohydrates for twenty-three days, had begun to cannibalize itself, flooding her veins with acids that burned like battery fluid. If your patient swore she was eating enough, would you believe her? The woman was thirty-two years old, white, and had no history of diabetes. She had given birth ten months earlier and was still breastfeeding her son. Before the diet, she had been healthy—no hospital admissions, no chronic conditions, no medications beyond the occasional ibuprofen for a headache. Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated, her delivery routine. She had returned to work part-time, balancing office hours with feedings, and described her energy as normal. Friends had mentioned low-carb diets as a way to lose the last of the baby weight without affecting milk supply. She had read the same advice online: fewer carbs, more fat, more protein. It was supposed to be safe. She tracked her intake carefully, aiming for fewer than twenty grams of carbohydrates a day, replacing bread with avocado, pasta with zucchini, sugar with stevia. She drank water, took her prenatal vitamins, and felt fine—until she didn’t. The first sign was nausea. It started on the eighth day. She assumed it was a stomach bug, something her son might have brought home from daycare. She drank ginger tea, ate crackers when she could, and waited for it to pass. By the tenth day, the nausea had worsened. She vomited twice in the morning, once after lunch, and once more in the evening. She still had no fever, no diarrhea, no abdominal pain. Her breasts felt full, her milk supply unchanged. She checked her temperature: 36.8°C. Her pulse was 88, her blood pressure 112/70. She called her midwife, who suggested hydration and rest. She tried electrolyte drinks, bone broth, small portions of chicken. Nothing stayed down. By the afternoon of the eleventh day, she could no longer keep water down. Her husband drove her to the emergency department. In the triage bay, her vitals were stable. Temperature 36.9°C, heart rate 92, blood pressure 108/68, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She looked tired but not acutely ill. The nurse noted dry mucous membranes and a capillary refill of three seconds. A venous blood gas was drawn. The result came back twenty minutes later: pH 7.20, base excess -19, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L. The emergency physician reviewed the numbers. Metabolic acidosis, severe. The differential was long: sepsis, diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, toxic ingestion, renal failure. The team ordered a full metabolic panel, a complete blood count, blood cultures, a chest X-ray, and a urine dipstick. They started intravenous normal saline at 200 milliliters per hour. The patient was moved to a monitored bed. The first misdiagnosis came quickly. The blood glucose was 5.2 mmol/L—normal. The urine dipstick showed ketones, but no glucose. The chest X-ray was clear. The white cell count was 9.8, the C-reactive protein 4. The emergency physician leaned toward a viral gastroenteritis with dehydration. The patient was given ondansetron for nausea, more fluids, and admitted to the medical ward for observation. 

Subscribe. Almost nobody has seen a presentation like this.

 Over the next six hours, she vomited three more times. Her urine output dropped to 20 milliliters per hour. A repeat venous blood gas showed worsening acidosis: pH 7.15, base excess -22. The bicarbonate had fallen to 6 mmol/L. The lactate was 1.2 mmol/L—normal. The anion gap was 28 mEq/L—elevated. The team added thiamine 100 milligrams intravenously and dextrose 5% at 125 milliliters per hour, suspecting alcoholic ketoacidosis, though the patient denied any alcohol use. She had never drunk more than a glass of wine with dinner, and none in the past month. The husband confirmed it. The team ordered a toxicology screen for ethanol, methanol, ethylene glycol, and salicylates. It came back negative for all substances. The second misdiagnosis followed. The medical registrar considered starvation ketoacidosis. The patient had been vomiting for two days, unable to keep food down. But she had no history of eating disorder, no rapid weight loss, no prior episodes. Her weight at admission was 68.2 kilograms, unchanged from her six-week postpartum check. She had been consuming approximately 1,500 kilocalories per day, with 18 grams of carbohydrates, 120 grams of protein, and 100 grams of fat. The team increased the dextrose concentration to 10%, delivering 50 grams of glucose over four hours. The acidosis persisted. A repeat blood gas at midnight showed pH 7.10, base excess -24, bicarbonate 5 mmol/L. The patient was now drowsy, though still oriented. She complained of muscle cramps in her calves and thighs. Her potassium was 3.1 mmol/L, corrected to 3.8 after 40 milliequivalents of potassium chloride. Her sodium was 132 mmol/L, chloride 98 mmol/L, magnesium 0.7 mmol/L. The team corrected the electrolytes and ordered a renal ultrasound. It showed normal kidney size, cortical thickness, and echogenicity, with no signs of obstruction or nephrocalcinosis. The nephrologist on call reviewed the case. He noted the normal creatinine of 62 micromoles per liter, the absence of proteinuria on urine dipstick, and the normal blood pressure. He suggested a trial of sodium bicarbonate infusion at 150 milliequivalents in 500 milliliters of normal saline over four hours. The pH rose transiently to 7.18 but fell back to 7.12 within two hours. The third misdiagnosis was the most dangerous. The intensivist was called at 3 a.m. The patient’s respiratory rate had risen to 28 breaths per minute, her heart rate to 110 beats per minute. She was now breathing deeply, her breaths labored, with a Kussmaul pattern. The intensivist suspected sepsis, though the blood cultures were still pending and the lactate remained 1.3 mmol/L. He ordered piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 grams intravenously and requested a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast. The scan showed no abscess, no obstruction, no free fluid, and normal enhancement of the liver, spleen, and kidneys. The blood cultures came back negative at 48 hours. The antibiotics were stopped. The acidosis was worse: pH 7.05, base excess -26, bicarbonate 4 mmol/L. The beta-hydroxybutyrate level, drawn at 4 a.m., returned at 7.8 mmol/L—far above the normal range of less than 0.6. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit. The intensivist considered intubation, but the patient was still protecting her airway, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14. He started a norepinephrine infusion at 0.05 micrograms per kilogram per minute to support her blood pressure, which had fallen to 88/50. The central venous pressure was 6 millimeters of mercury. The team was running out of explanations. Stop for a second. If you're still watching, ask yourself: what would you test next? 

Subscribe to No Known Cause before the mechanism is revealed.

 The blood sugar is normal. The ketones are high. The lactate is fine. The scans are clear. What’s left? Dr. Vasquez was the endocrinologist on call. She reviewed the chart at 6 a.m. The patient had been in the hospital for eighteen hours. Three working diagnoses, three failed treatments. The blood glucose was still 5.1 mmol/L. The ketones were still present at 3+ on urine dipstick. The acidosis was still severe. Dr. Vasquez asked the nurse for a detailed dietary history. The patient had been following a low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet for eleven days. She had been breastfeeding throughout, producing approximately 700 milliliters of milk per day, measured by pre- and post-feed weights. Dr. Vasquez ordered a serum beta-hydroxybutyrate. It came back at 6.2 mmol/L—markedly elevated. She also ordered a serum acetoacetate, which returned at 1.8 mmol/L, and a urine acetone level, which was 2+. The diagnosis clicked. The patient did not have diabetes. She had euglycemic ketoacidosis—a rare but recognized complication of low-carbohydrate diets in breastfeeding women. The mechanism was straightforward, once seen. Breastfeeding requires glucose. The mammary glands take up glucose from the bloodstream to produce lactose, the primary sugar in milk. Lactose synthesis consumes approximately 50 to 75 grams of glucose per day, depending on milk volume. In this patient, the demand was at the higher end, given her milk production of 700 milliliters daily. A low-carbohydrate diet forces the body to rely on fat for energy. Fat breakdown produces ketones—acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetone. Normally, the body can use ketones for fuel, and the blood pH remains stable. But breastfeeding creates a unique metabolic demand. When carbohydrate intake is severely restricted, the body cannot produce enough glucose through gluconeogenesis to meet both maternal and lactational needs. The liver ramps up fat breakdown, producing more ketones than the body can clear. The ketones accumulate, the blood becomes acidic, and the patient develops ketoacidosis—despite normal blood sugar. The team tested this hypothesis step by step. First, they measured the patient’s insulin level, which was 12 microunits per milliliter—normal, ruling out insulin deficiency. Next, they checked her glucagon level, which was 180 picograms per milliliter—elevated, consistent with a counterregulatory response to low carbohydrate intake. They calculated her glucose production rate using a stable isotope technique, which showed a rate of 12 micromoles per kilogram per minute—below the expected 15 to 20 for a breastfeeding woman. 

Subscribe to No Known Cause. Every case is a documented first report.

 Finally, they measured her milk lactose concentration, which was 6.8 grams per 100 milliliters—normal, confirming that her mammary glands were still functioning but starved of substrate. The treatment was simple. The team stopped the low-carb diet. They started intravenous dextrose at 10% concentration, providing 200 grams of glucose per day. They continued insulin at a low dose of 0.5 units per hour—not to lower blood sugar, but to suppress fat breakdown and ketone production. Within two hours, the beta-hydroxybutyrate level fell to 4.1 mmol/L. By six hours, the acidosis began to improve. The pH rose to 7.25, the bicarbonate to 12 mmol/L. The patient’s nausea eased. She was able to drink 100 milliliters of water without vomiting. By twelve hours, her pH was 7.35, her bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, and her beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.9 mmol/L. She was transferred back to the medical ward. The next morning, she was eating a normal diet—carbohydrates included, with 250 grams of glucose-rich foods. Her milk supply remained normal, with no change in volume or lactose concentration. She was discharged on the third day, with instructions to consume at least 150 grams of carbohydrates per day while breastfeeding. Her son continued to breastfeed without interruption. This case changed how clinicians think about low-carbohydrate diets in breastfeeding women. Before, the risk of ketoacidosis was considered theoretical. Guidelines had warned about the possibility, but few cases had been reported. This patient’s presentation was severe, but her recovery was rapid once the diagnosis was made. The authors of the case report argued that the metabolic stress of lactation makes breastfeeding women uniquely vulnerable to ketoacidosis on low-carb diets. They recommended that clinicians ask about dietary habits in any breastfeeding woman presenting with unexplained nausea, vomiting, or fatigue—even if blood sugar is normal. The case also highlighted the importance of considering euglycemic ketoacidosis in the differential diagnosis of metabolic acidosis, regardless of the patient’s diet. It was a reminder that what is safe for one person may not be safe for another—and that the body’s response to a simple dietary change can be anything but simple. For anyone who wants to go deeper, our companion resource on metabolic adaptations in lactation is linked below. If this case made you see something new, you know what to do. --- Subscribe to this channel for more documented cases.

real_cases.title: Post-COVID-19 vaccine Guillain-Barré syndrome; first reported case from Qatar.
real_cases.summary: Abstract Introduction Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an immune-mediated peripheral neuropathy that was reported following meningococcus, polio, influenza and rabies vaccines. However, an association with the COVID-19 vaccine is yet to be established. Presentation of case We present the case of an elderly gentleman with no history of SARS-CoV-2 infection or any recent viral or bacterial illnesses who presented with GBS 20 days after the second dose of COVID-19 vaccination. The diagnosis was established based on physical examination, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine, cerebrospinal
real_cases.citation: Razok A, Shams A, Almeer A, Zahid M. Post-COVID-19 vaccine Guillain-Barré syndrome; first reported case from Qatar. Annals of medicine and surgery (2012) 2021 doi:10.1016/j.amsu.2021.102540 — licensed CC BY

He ordered piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 grams intravenously and requested a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast. The scan showed no abscess, no obstruction, no free fluid, and normal enhancement of the liver, spleen, and kidneys. The blood cultures came back negative at 48 hours. The antibiotics were stopped. The acidosis was worse: pH 7.05, base excess -26, bicarbonate 4 mmol/L. The beta-hydroxybutyrate level, drawn at 4 a.m., returned at 7.8 mmol/L—far above the normal range of less than 0.6. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit. The intensivist considered intubation, but the patient was still protecting her airway, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14. He started a norepinephrine infusion at 0.05 micrograms per kilogram per minute to support her blood pressure, which had fallen to 88/50. The central venous pressure was 6 millimeters of mercury. The team was running out of explanations. Stop for a second. If you're still watching, ask yourself: what would you test next? 

Subscribe to No Known Cause before the mechanism is revealed.

 The blood sugar is normal. The ketones are high. The lactate is fine. The scans are clear. What’s left? Dr. Vasquez was the endocrinologist on call. She reviewed the chart at 6 a.m. The patient had been in the hospital for eighteen hours. Three working diagnoses, three failed treatments. The blood glucose was still 5.1 mmol/L. The ketones were still present at 3+ on urine dipstick. The acidosis was still severe. Dr. Vasquez asked the nurse for a detailed dietary history. The patient had been following a low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet for eleven days. She had been breastfeeding throughout, producing approximately 700 milliliters of milk per day, measured by pre- and post-feed weights. Dr. Vasquez ordered a serum beta-hydroxybutyrate. It came back at 6.2 mmol/L—markedly elevated. She also ordered a serum acetoacetate, which returned at 1.8 mmol/L, and a urine acetone level, which was 2+. The diagnosis clicked. The patient did not have diabetes. She had euglycemic ketoacidosis—a rare but recognized complication of low-carbohydrate diets in breastfeeding women. The mechanism was straightforward, once seen. Breastfeeding requires glucose. The mammary glands take up glucose from the bloodstream to produce lactose, the primary sugar in milk. Lactose synthesis consumes approximately 50 to 75 grams of glucose per day, depending on milk volume. In this patient, the demand was at the higher end, given her milk production of 700 milliliters daily. A low-carbohydrate diet forces the body to rely on fat for energy. Fat breakdown produces ketones—acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetone. Normally, the body can use ketones for fuel, and the blood pH remains stable. But breastfeeding creates a unique metabolic demand. When carbohydrate intake is severely restricted, the body cannot produce enough glucose through gluconeogenesis to meet both maternal and lactational needs. The liver ramps up fat breakdown, producing more ketones than the body can clear. The ketones accumulate, the blood becomes acidic, and the patient develops ketoacidosis—despite normal blood sugar. The team tested this hypothesis step by step. First, they measured the patient’s insulin level, which was 12 microunits per milliliter—normal, ruling out insulin deficiency. Next, they checked her glucagon level, which was 180 picograms per milliliter—elevated, consistent with a counterregulatory response to low carbohydrate intake. They calculated her glucose production rate using a stable isotope technique, which showed a rate of 12 micromoles per kilogram per minute—below the expected 15 to 20 for a breastfeeding woman.

 Finally, they measured her milk lactose concentration, which was 6.8 grams per 100 milliliters—normal, confirming that her mammary glands were still functioning but starved of substrate. The treatment was simple. The team stopped the low-carb diet. They started intravenous dextrose at 10% concentration, providing 200 grams of glucose per day. They continued insulin at a low dose of 0.5 units per hour—not to lower blood sugar, but to suppress fat breakdown and ketone production. Within two hours, the beta-hydroxybutyrate level fell to 4.1 mmol/L. By six hours, the acidosis began to improve. The pH rose to 7.25, the bicarbonate to 12 mmol/L. The patient’s nausea eased. She was able to drink 100 milliliters of water without vomiting. By twelve hours, her pH was 7.35, her bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, and her beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.9 mmol/L. She was transferred back to the medical ward. The next morning, she was eating a normal diet—carbohydrates included, with 250 grams of glucose-rich foods. Her milk supply remained normal, with no change in volume or lactose concentration. She was discharged on the third day, with instructions to consume at least 150 grams of carbohydrates per day while breastfeeding. Her son continued to breastfeed without interruption. This case changed how clinicians think about low-carbohydrate diets in breastfeeding women. Before, the risk of ketoacidosis was considered theoretical. Guidelines had warned about the possibility, but few cases had been reported. This patient’s presentation was severe, but her recovery was rapid once the diagnosis was made. The authors of the case report argued that the metabolic stress of lactation makes breastfeeding women uniquely vulnerable to ketoacidosis on low-carb diets. They recommended that clinicians ask about dietary habits in any breastfeeding woman presenting with unexplained nausea, vomiting, or fatigue—even if blood sugar is normal. The case also highlighted the importance of considering euglycemic ketoacidosis in the differential diagnosis of metabolic acidosis, regardless of the patient’s diet. It was a reminder that what is safe for one person may not be safe for another—and that the body’s response to a simple dietary change can be anything but simple. real_cases.summary: Abstract Introduction Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an immune-mediated peripheral neuropathy that was reported following meningococcus, polio, influenza and rabies vaccines. However, an association with the COVID-19 vaccine is yet to be established. Presentation of case We present the case of an elderly gentleman with no history of SARS-CoV-2 infection or any recent viral or bacterial illnesses who presented with GBS 20 days after the second dose of COVID-19 vaccination.
